title: Node.js Debugging & Observability Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on structured logging with pino, request IDs, debugging with node --inspect and Chrome DevTools, --watch, heap-snapshot leak diagnosis, and signal handling with graceful shutdown.

chapters.title: Observability and Debugging: The Mental Model
points: Structured logging = one JSON object per line (level, time, msg, plus fields), so logs are machine-searchable instead of free-text strings
Three debugging tools, three jobs: logs (what happened in prod), inspector (step through live code), heap snapshots (why memory grows)
Log to stdout only; the platform (Docker, systemd, k8s) collects and ships logs, the app should not manage files or rotation
console.log vs pino: console.log is synchronous-ish, unstructured, has no levels or child context; pino is fast, JSON, leveled
Common mistake: string-concatenated logs like 'user ' + id; instead pass fields as an object so they stay queryable

chapters.title: Pino and Log Levels
points: Setup: const logger = require('pino')({ level: process.env.LOG_LEVEL || 'info' }); call logger.info({ userId }, 'login ok'), with the object first and the message second
Level order low to high: trace 10, debug 20, info 30, warn 40, error 50, fatal 60; a level logs itself and everything above it
Log errors as logger.error({ err }, 'payment failed'); pino's err serializer keeps type, message and stack, while logging a plain string loses the stack
redact: ['req.headers.authorization', 'password'] masks secrets in output; never log tokens, passwords or full card data
pino-pretty for dev only (node app.js | pino-pretty); piping or transports in production add cost and defeat raw JSON shipping

chapters.title: Request IDs and Child Loggers
points: Request ID = unique ID per incoming request, attached to every log line so one request's logs can be filtered across the whole flow
Reuse the incoming x-request-id header if present, otherwise generate one with crypto.randomUUID(); echo it back in the response header
Child logger: const reqLog = logger.child({ reqId }) adds the field to every line it writes, with no repeated passing of fields
Passing the logger through every function is tedious: AsyncLocalStorage (node:async_hooks) stores the per-request logger and reads it anywhere in the async call chain
Forward the ID on outbound calls (x-request-id header) so logs correlate across services; a missing ID in downstream services breaks the trace

chapters.title: node --inspect, DevTools and --watch
points: node --inspect app.js starts the V8 inspector on 127.0.0.1:9229; --inspect-brk pauses on the first line so you can set breakpoints before startup code runs
Attach from Chrome via chrome://inspect then click inspect on the target, or open the Node.js icon in any DevTools window; VS Code attach also works on port 9229
DevTools Sources: set breakpoints, conditional breakpoints, logpoints (log without editing code), step over/into/out, and watch the call stack and scope variables
Never expose the inspector on 0.0.0.0 (--inspect=0.0.0.0:9229): it gives remote code execution; reach remote hosts via an SSH tunnel (ssh -L 9229:127.0.0.1:9229)
node --watch app.js restarts on file changes (Node 18.11+ and stable in 22); --watch-path=./src limits what is watched; it restarts the process and does not hot-reload, so in-memory state is lost

chapters.title: Diagnosing Memory Leaks and Graceful Shutdown
points: Leak signature: heapUsed (process.memoryUsage()) keeps climbing after garbage collection and never returns to a baseline; a sawtooth that stays level is healthy

Three-snapshot technique in DevTools Memory tab: take snapshot, run the workload, snapshot, run it again, snapshot; use the 'Objects allocated between Snapshot 1 and 2' filter and sort by Retained Size
Read the Retainers pane to see what holds an object; typical culprits are unbounded Maps and caches, listeners never removed (emitter.on in a request handler), and closures or global arrays
Signals: SIGTERM is the polite stop sent by Docker, Kubernetes and systemd; SIGINT is Ctrl+C; SIGKILL cannot be caught. Handle with process.on('SIGTERM', shutdown)

Graceful shutdown order: stop accepting (server.close()), finish in-flight requests, close DB and queue connections, then process.exit(0); add a force-exit timer (setTimeout(...).unref()) shorter than the platform grace period (k8s default 30s)

chapters.title: Node Debugging and Shutdown Cheat Sheet
points: Levels: trace 10, debug 20, info 30, warn 40, error 50, fatal 60; logger.info({ obj }, 'msg'); logger.child({ reqId }); redact: [paths]
Inspect commands: node --inspect, --inspect-brk, chrome://inspect, --watch, --watch-path=./src; the inspector stays on localhost
Leak workflow: 3 snapshots, filter allocated between 1 and 2, sort by Retained Size, read Retainers
Shutdown skeleton: on SIGTERM -> server.close() -> close DB -> exit(0), with an unref'd force-exit timer
Mistake checklist: logging secrets, string-concatenated logs, no request ID, exposed inspector port, no SIGTERM handler (the process gets SIGKILLed after the grace period)
